1.pericope_label: And Moses spake unto the heads of the tribes concerning the children of Israel, saying, This is the thing which the Lord hath commanded. If a man vow a vow unto the Lord, or swear an oath to bind his soul with a bond; he shall not break his word, he shall do according to all that proceedeth out of his mouth.

schools.summary: Put the general rule at the head and parse its two terms, since the whole chapter turns on the distinction. If any one vow a vow to Jehovah, or swear an oath to bind his soul to abstinence, he shall not break his word but shall do according to all that has gone out of his mouth; that is, he shall keep or fulfil both the vow and the promise of abstinence in perfect accordance with what he said. The first noun is a positive vow, a promise to give or to sanctify some part of one's property to the Lord. The second comes from a verb meaning to bind or fetter, and is the negative vow, the vow of abstinence, the idiom being to take an abstinence upon his soul. Note what the text does not say: in what such abstinence consisted is nowhere explained, and the silence is not an oversight but a sign that the practice was well understood from traditional custom; in all probability it consisted chiefly in fasting and other similar abstinence from things otherwise lawful. Confirm the distinction from the way the words are used elsewhere. The Nazarite's vow, which is generally reckoned among the vows of abstinence, is nevertheless called by the first noun and not the second, which shows that the classification follows the form of the undertaking and not merely its content. Keep the two categories in hand through the rest of the chapter, because every case that follows concerns one or the other, and the ratification or annulment described later applies to both alike.

Begin by naming the point the chapter exists to make, that vows made by persons who are not their own masters do not hold good before God. Then show why the general law is restated before the exception: he repeats it first so that no one should think there is any contradiction in what follows, as much as to say that the rule stands good, but that it refers only to such as are their own masters, women and girls under the power of another not being free to promise without the concurrence of a father or a husband. Guard the whole with a condition. The preface must be understood of lawful vows only, whereby neither is religion corrupted nor the holiness of God's name profaned; for unless what we offer is acceptable to God, there can be no obligation upon the conscience at all. State the same limit from the other side, that the matter must be something lawful, not contrary to the revealed will and mind of God, tending to the glory of God, the honour of religion, the service of the sanctuary, or the good of a man himself or of his neighbour, or else something purely indifferent which may or may not be done without offence. Report the rabbinic formulation of that limit, that a man may forbid himself what is already forbidden, and may forbid what is free and lawful, but may not make free or lawful what is forbidden, since such a vow will not stand. Then raise the case the text omits. No mention is made of male children, and since their condition was the same it seems they must be included with the daughters and wives, unless God chose to pay regard to the weaker sex; and since he permits females not under a father's power to vow in spite of their sex, and does not make sex an excuse for levity or thoughtlessness, the object proposed seems to have been that the right of the father over his children, and of the husband over his wife, should be maintained inviolate. On the age at which a promise begins to bind, give the traditions and then decline to press the matter: thirteen years by one Targum, twelve by the Mishnah, while it may probably be conjectured that boys of ten, though still united with their family, are bound by what they say. Do not contend pertinaciously about it, since it is better to leave undecided whatever is doubtful.

Define the thing before regulating it: a vow is a religious promise made to God. Then set out the kinds, so the reader knows the range of what follows. There were vows of abstinence or humiliation, of which this chapter speaks later; the vow of the Nazarite; vows of giving certain things or sacrifices to the Lord; and vows of alms given to the poor. Having classified them, judge the law itself, and judge it favourably on two counts at once. It must have been very useful, since it both prevented and annulled rash vows, and at the same time provided a proper sanction for the support and performance of those that were rationally and piously made; the same statute therefore restrains folly and secures sincerity, which is not a common combination in law. Add a third benefit that is easily missed: it must have acted as a great preventive of lying and hypocrisy, since a man who knew his word could be tested was less likely to give it lightly. Then state the obligation without softening it. If a vow was properly made, a man or woman was bound, under penalty of the displeasure of God, to fulfil it; the power of annulment given later to a father or a husband is a limit on who may bind himself, not a licence to the person bound. Keep both halves of that in view, because the chapter is commonly read for its exceptions when its first business is to insist that what is promised to God is to be paid.

Ask first why this law was delivered to the heads of the tribes rather than to the congregation, and answer that they might instruct those who were under their charge, explain the law to them, give them the necessary cautions, and call them to account, if there were occasion, for the breach of their vows; and allow the guess that the heads of the tribes had, upon some emergency of this kind, consulted Moses and desired by him to know the mind of God, and are here told it. Then state the case supposed. A person vows a vow unto the Lord, making God a party to the promise and designing his honour and glory in it. The matter of the vow is supposed to be something lawful, for no man can be by his own promise bound to do what he is already by the divine precept prohibited from doing; yet it is supposed to be something which, in such measures and degrees, was not a necessary duty antecedent to the vow. Give examples, so the reader can recognise the kind: a man might vow to bring such sacrifices at certain times, to give such a sum or proportion in alms, to forbear meats and drinks which the law allowed, or to fast and afflict the soul at other times besides the day of atonement; and many such vows might be made in an extraordinary heat of holy zeal, in humiliation for sin committed, for the prevention of sin, in the pursuit of some mercy desired, or in gratitude for some mercy received. Say that it is of great use to make such vows, provided they be made in sincerity and with due caution, and cite the Jewish doctors, who call vows the hedge of separation, that is, a fence to religion. Then take the phrase that carries the chapter. He that vows is said to bind his soul with a bond: it is a vow to God, who is a spirit, and to him the soul, with all its powers, must be bound; a promise to man is a bond upon the estate, but a promise to God is a bond upon the soul. Distinguish the two sorts we make now. Our sacramental vows bind us to no more than what was before our duty, and neither father nor husband can disannul them; our occasional vows concern what before was in our own power, and once made are bonds upon the soul likewise. Finally press the command: he shall not break his word, though afterwards he may change his mind, but shall do according to what he has said. The margin reads, he shall not profane his word, and vowing is an ordinance of God, so that to vow in hypocrisy is to profane that ordinance. It is plainly determined that it is better not to vow than to vow and not pay. Be not deceived, God is not mocked: his promises to us are yea and amen, and let not ours to him be yea and nay.

debates.question: At what age does a person's own vow begin to bind?

sides.position: Thirteen years, by the Targum of Jonathan, and twelve by the Mishnah
Under twelve for a girl and under thirteen for a young man, such persons having no power to vow away another's property
Probably boys of ten are bound though still in the family; but the point is doubtful and not worth contending for

debates.question: Why are male children not mentioned?

sides.position: Their condition being the same, they seem to be included with the daughters and wives — unless God chose to regard the weaker sex
Some think, probably enough, that the rule extends to a son at home under tutors; but we may not make distinctions the law does not

outliers.note: Alone distinguishes the two sorts of vow a Christian now makes: sacramental vows, which bind to no more than what was already duty and which neither father nor husband can disannul, and occasional vows concerning what was before in a man's own power.

Alone observes that the text never explains what the abstinence consisted in, and reads the silence as evidence that traditional custom made it plain — probably fasting and similar refusal of otherwise lawful things.

3.pericope_label: If a woman also vow a vow unto the Lord, and bind herself by a bond, being in her father's house in her youth; And her father hear her vow, and her bond wherewith she hath bound her soul, and her father shall hold his peace at her: then all her vows shall stand, and every bond wherewith she hath bound her soul shall stand. But if her father disallow her in the day that he heareth; not any of her vows, or of her bonds wherewith she hath bound her soul, shall stand: and the Lord shall forgive her, because her father disallowed her. And if she had at all an husband, when she vowed, or uttered ought out of her lips, wherewith she bound her soul; And her husband heard it, and held his peace at her in the day that he heard it: then her vows shall stand, and her bonds wherewith she bound her soul shall stand. But if her husband disallowed her on the day that he heard it; then he shall make her vow which she vowed, and that which she uttered with her lips, wherewith she bound her soul, of none effect: and the Lord shall forgive her.

schools.summary: Number the cases before expounding any of them, since the section is a set of parallel rulings and the reader will lose his way otherwise. Four distinct cases are contemplated in regard to vows taken by women: that of an unmarried woman living, in her youth, in the house of her father; that of a woman unmarried at the time of making a vow, who enters into the state of marriage before the vow is fulfilled; that of a widow or of a divorced woman; and that of a married woman. Say what the section is doing as a whole: the sanctity and obligations of the fifth commandment are distinctly recognised and enforced in these verses. Then take the first case. If a woman in her youth, still unmarried and living in her father's house, made a vow of performance or of abstinence, and her father heard of it and remained silent, it was to stand and remain in force; but if he held her back when he heard of it, that is, forbade her fulfilling it, it was not to stand, and Jehovah would forgive her because of her father's refusal. State the principle underneath the ruling, since it is the reason the case is decided as it is: obedience to a father stood higher than a self-imposed religious service. Explain the clause about forgiveness in the same practical way, that she would not incur the guilt or the punishment which would otherwise have been incurred by neglecting to fulfil what she had promised. Then take the second case, of a vow of performance or abstinence made by a woman before her marriage and brought along with her into it, so that the words are better rendered, and if she should be married to a husband whilst her vows are upon her, or the rash utterance of her lips wherewith she hath bound her soul. In such a case the husband had to decide as to its validity in the same way as the father. Note the word rendered rash utterance, whose cognate verb occurs in the law of the guilt offering and seems to denote something uttered without reflection; and keep the case distinct from the one treated later, of a woman who takes a vow after she is already married.

Take the two cases in order and let the ruling in each turn on silence. If a daughter, while living with her father, has vowed anything without his knowledge, it is of no force; the same holds if the father, hearing the vow, has disallowed it; but if he has held his peace, his silence is declared to be equivalent to consent. Draw the general lesson from that at once, since it reaches further than the case: all those who are possessed of power do not do their duty unless they frankly and discreetly express their opposition whenever anything displeases them, for their connivance is a kind of tacit approbation. Then treat married women, whose vows made in the absence or with the disapproval of their husbands are of none effect, but which they are obliged to perform if the husbands have known of them and been silent; for many deceptions might otherwise arise, since it is usual with many, when they wish to gratify their wives, to conceal their opinion for the time and then, when the period of actual performance arrives, to elude what may have been promised. Say plainly what such a man deserves: unless they use their privilege in proper time, God would have them bear the punishment of their servile indulgence and dissimulation. Note that the same rule guards against the opposite fault, since women are often urged to deceive by levity and inconstancy, and a woman may make a vow in the precipitate fervour of her zeal and afterwards retract it under the specious pretext that she was not then free and her own mistress. Since instances of this wicked change of mind are too frequent, God declares that the period when the vow was made is to be considered, so that they are no less liable than if their condition had remained the same. Then handle the detail of the day, and make it argue for the rule rather than against it: when the dissent of the father or the husband is required on the same day, it is tantamount to saying that what they have once approved of cannot afterwards be disallowed. Finally, weigh the words of forgiveness carefully. The expression is remarkable, and the Lord shall forgive her, whereby Moses gently reproves the foolish thoughtlessness of the girl; and surely their rashness is worthy of reprehension if, unmindful of their condition, they as it were shake off the yoke and hastily commit themselves. God therefore hints that they are not without blame; but lest they should be tormented by secret remorse, he removes every scruple, declaring that he will forgive if the performance has been prevented from some other quarter.

Fix the ages first, since the case depends on them. In her youth means, say the rabbins, under twelve years of age, and under thirteen in the case of a young man; young persons of that age were considered to be under the authority of their parents, and had consequently no power to vow away the property of another, and a married woman was in the same circumstances because she was under the authority of her husband. Then state the mechanism plainly. If the parents or the husband heard of the vow and objected to it on the same day on which they heard of it, the vow was annulled; but if, having heard of it, they held their peace, this was considered a ratification. Be exact about how that day is reckoned, for the whole practical force of the law is in it: the time allowed for disallowing the vow was not to be counted from her vowing but from his knowledge of her vow, and it means speedily, or without delay, allowing only convenient time for deliberation. Then interpret the clause of forgiveness, and set its limit carefully, since the limit is where the law is most likely to be abused. The Lord will forgive her the not performing of it; but this should be understood only of vows which could not be performed without invading the father's right. If one should vow to forbear such and such a sin, and all the occasions and means leading to it, and to perform such and such duties when he had opportunity, no father can discharge him from vows of that kind. Reinforce the point from the other direction with the maxim that a rash vow was never to be kept, for, as Philo says, and common sense and justice say the same, he who commits an unjust action because of his vow adds one crime to another, first by making an unlawful vow and then by doing an unlawful action. Close on the application to households now. If this law does not extend to children's marrying without their parents' consent, so far as to put it in the power of the parent to disannul the marriage, which some think it does, yet it certainly proves the sinfulness of such marriages, and obliges those children to repent and humble themselves before God and their parents.

Set the exception against the rule before taking the cases. It is taken for granted that all persons who are at their own disposal, and likewise of sound understanding and memory, are bound to perform whatever they vow that is lawful and possible; but if the person vowing be under the dominion and at the disposal of another, the case is different, and two cases much alike are here put and determined. Take the daughter first, and admit the limits of what may be inferred: some think, probably enough, that the rule extends to a son likewise while he is at home and under tutors and governors, but whether the exception may be stretched so far cannot be said, since we are not allowed to make distinctions which the law does not. Her vow is in suspense until her father knows of it, and knows it from her, for when it comes to his knowledge it is in his power either to ratify or to nullify it. Then argue the case in favour of the vow, taking the two possibilities in order. Even his silence shall suffice to ratify it, for silence gives consent; by saying nothing he allows his daughter the liberty she has assumed, and so long as he says nothing against it she shall be bound. But his protestation shall perfectly disannul it, and give the reasons why he might reasonably protest: such a vow may be prejudicial to the affairs of the family, may break the father's measures, may perplex the provision made for his table if the vow related to meats, or lessen the provision made for his children if it would be more expensive than his estate would bear; and in any case it was an infringement of his authority over his child. If he disallow it she is discharged, and the Lord shall forgive her, that is, she shall not be charged with the guilt of violating her vow, for she showed her good-will in making it, and if her intentions were sincere she shall be accounted better than sacrifice. Then draw the public lesson, which is the real weight of the passage. This shows how great a deference children owe to their parents, and how much they ought to honour them and be obedient to them; and it is for the interest of the public that the paternal authority be supported, for when children are countenanced in their disobedience to their parents, as they were by the tradition of the elders, they soon become in other things children of Belial. Say lastly what the wife's case adds: she has nothing that she can strictly call her own but with her husband's allowance, and if he disallow her vow, her obligation to him takes place of an obligation that arose purely from her own act and not from any prior command of God, so that it would now be her sin to disobey him.

debates.question: How is the day for disallowing the vow reckoned?

sides.position: From the day he hears it, not the next and still less a third or fourth; and it might be done on a sabbath
Not from her vowing but from his knowledge of it, allowing only convenient time for deliberation
That the dissent is required the same day amounts to saying that what has once been approved cannot afterwards be disallowed

debates.question: How far does the release reach?

sides.position: Only to vows that could not be performed without invading the father's right; no father can discharge a child from a promise to forsake sin or do a duty
She is not charged with the guilt of violating it: she showed good-will, and sincere intentions are accounted better than sacrifice
She does not incur the guilt or punishment otherwise incurred by leaving the vow unfulfilled
A rebuke is folded into the pardon: Moses gently reproves her thoughtlessness, and God hints she is not blameless while removing the scruple
A rash vow was never to be kept, since a man who acts unjustly on account of his vow adds one crime to another

outliers.note: Alone turns the father's silence into a rule for everyone in authority: no one does his duty unless he frankly and discreetly opposes what displeases him, since connivance is a kind of tacit approbation.

Alone brings in Philo against the keeping of rash vows, on the ground that a man who commits an unjust action because of his vow adds one crime to another, first by making an unlawful vow and then by doing an unlawful act.

if her father disallow her in the day that he heareth
the LORD shall forgive her, because her father disallowed her

9.pericope_label: But every vow of a widow, and of her that is divorced, wherewith they have bound their souls, shall stand against her. And if she vowed in her husband's house, or bound her soul by a bond with an oath; And her husband heard it, and held his peace at her, and disallowed her not: then all her vows shall stand, and every bond wherewith she bound her soul shall stand. But if her husband hath utterly made them void on the day he heard them; then whatsoever proceeded out of her lips concerning her vows, or concerning the bond of her soul, shall not stand: her husband hath made them void; and the Lord shall forgive her. Every vow, and every binding oath to afflict the soul, her husband may establish it, or her husband may make it void. But if her husband altogether hold his peace at her from day to day; then he establisheth all her vows, or all her bonds, which are upon her: he confirmeth them, because he held his peace at her in the day that he heard them. But if he shall any ways make them void after that he hath heard them; then he shall bear her iniquity. These are the statutes, which the Lord commanded Moses, between a man and his wife, between the father and his daughter, being yet in her youth in her father's house.

schools.summary: Keep the classification in view to the end, since the last section returns to it. Reference is again made to the two kinds of vows treated of in this chapter, namely a vow to do anything and a vow to abstain from anything, and the rule about ratification and annulment applies to both alike; the mention of afflicting the soul is an instance of the second kind and not a restriction of the husband's power to that kind only. On the tenth verse, render it simply as the case of a woman who took a vow of performance or of abstinence whilst in the house of her husband, and keep it distinct from the case already treated, of a woman who came into her marriage already under a vow. The distinction is not pedantry: the earlier case asks what a husband may do about an obligation contracted before he had any authority, while this one asks what he may do about one contracted under it, and the law answers both the same way but for different reasons. Note that the widow and the divorced woman are set between the two married cases rather than at the end, which is the arrangement of a lawgiver working through degrees of dependence rather than through a narrative order, and that the closing verse names only the two relations which the whole chapter has been about, a man and his wife, and a father and his daughter while she is in her youth and in his house.

Explain first why the widow is expressly named, since the reason is not obvious and the whole force of the verse depends on it. She is named lest a woman should think that by a second marriage she would escape, as being no longer free and again under the yoke; for people often extricate themselves by such subtle excuses, and a woman who bound herself while subject to a husband might afterwards, when he is dead, retract under the specious pretext that she was not then free and her own mistress. The same trick could be worked the other way by a divorced woman who binds herself and then, having married, appears to herself to be released. God therefore declares that the period when the vow was made is what counts, so that such women are no less liable than if their condition had remained the same. Then set out what the Jewish authorities make of the betrothed woman, whose case the verse does not directly cover. One takes the Scripture to speak of a widow from marriage, that is, one who has actually been married; but where a woman has been only espoused and the husband dies, the power is transmitted back to the father. The Mishnah puts the rule as a pair of contrasts: if the father of such a betrothed person dies the power is not transmitted to the husband, but if the husband dies the power is transmitted to the father, so that in this case the power of a father is greater than that of a husband, while in others the power of a husband is greater, because a husband makes void the vow of a woman who is of age and a father does not. On the closing verse, state the purpose of the whole: this power of ratifying or disannulling vows, which a husband had over his wife and a father over his daughter, existed to prevent imprudent and extravagant vows and the too frequent use of them, the consequences of which might be bad in families. And correct one misreading before leaving the chapter. The words about the husband's house have been taken by some to refer to a household and its master, which is a very gross mistake: the subject itself does not admit of such an explanation, and the words of Moses forbid it, so that it is the more surprising that persons skilled in the Hebrew tongue have not seen the matter clearly.

Give the widow and the divorced woman their due first, and note the practical circumstance that makes the ruling necessary: such a woman stands bound by whatever she has promised, and this holds though she be in her father's house, whither such persons often returned. Then illustrate the tenth verse with a case, since the abstract rule is hard to feel. Suppose a woman, now a widow or divorced, made her vow while her husband still lived with her, promising that if she were left a widow she would give such a proportion of her estate to pious or charitable uses; she may repent of it when she comes to be a widow, and may believe, or persuade herself, that she is free from it because the promise was made in her husband's lifetime. Grant the release only on the condition the text gives: it holds if her husband then disallowed it, and is denied if by silence or otherwise he consented to it. On afflicting the soul, take it of fasting, watching or the like, and see why the words are added: they show that the husband had this power not only in those vows which concerned himself or his estate, but also in those which might seem only to concern her own person or body, the reason being that the wife's body is the husband's right, so that she might not do anything to its injury without his consent. Then press the clause that turns the obligation around. If he has heard the vow and approved it by his silence from day to day, and after that time shall hinder it, which he ought not to do, her non-performance shall be imputed to him and not to her; and set beside that the reminder that her life is at stake if she fulfil not the obligation under which she has laid herself. Close on the statute itself. It is very probable that this law, like that concerning the succession of daughters, rose from the exigency of some particular case that had just then occurred. Making vows, in almost any case, is a dangerous business; they seldom do any good and often much evil. He who does not feel himself bound to do what is fit, right and just from the standing testimony of God's word is not likely to do it from any obligation he may lay upon his own conscience; if God's word lack weight with him, his own will prove lighter than vanity. Yet do not end in mere caution: every man who professes the Christian religion is under the most solemn obligation to devote body, soul and spirit to God, not only to the utmost extent of his powers but as long as he exists, and baptism and the Lord's Supper are additional ratifications of that great general vow, which every true follower of Christ should always remember and frequently renew.

debates.question: Whose vow does the tenth verse describe?

sides.position: A betrothed woman, by the Targum's gloss; but Jarchi's reading of a married woman seems likelier
A woman who took her vow whilst already in her husband's house, as distinct from one who brought a vow into the marriage
A woman now widowed or divorced who vowed during her husband's lifetime, and who may not plead that she was unfree when she spoke

debates.question: Where does the guilt fall if the husband vetoes late?

sides.position: On him: having approved by silence day after day, if he then hinders it, her non-performance is imputed to him and not to her
Her life is at stake in the obligation she has laid upon herself
He expressed his dislike not at the time he heard it but some time afterwards — one day after, by the Targum

outliers.note: Alone works out why afflicting the soul is specified, namely to show that the husband's power reached even what seemed to concern her own body only, the wife's body being reckoned his right.

Alone attacks a rival construction of the tenth verse, in which the husband's house is read as a household and its master, calling it a very gross mistake that the subject does not admit and the words of Moses forbid.
